'''Karl Kraus''' (21 March 1938 – 9 June 1988) was a German [[theoretical physicist]] who made major contributions to the foundations of [[quantum physics]]. He is known for his work in [[quantum operation]]s, where [[Kraus operator]]s are named after him.

==Life==

Kraus was born in 1938 in Hohenelbe/Giant Mountains, today [[Vrchlabí]]. After the war, he grew up in [[Elsterwerda]] and attended local schools. He studied physics from 1955 to 1960 at the [[Humboldt University of Berlin]] (East) and the [[Free University of Berlin]] (West). He graduated in 1962 with a thesis about [[Hendrik Lorentz|Lorentz]]'s theory of gravity, carried out under the supervision of Kurt Just.<ref>Karl Kraus: ''Lorentzinvariante Gravitationstheorie'', Dissertation, Freie Universität Berlin, 1962.</ref> Kraus then joined as an assistant to Günther Ludwig at the [[University of Marburg]], where he qualified in 1966. In 1971, he accepted a professorship at the Institute of Physics of the [[University of Würzburg]], where he established a [[mathematical physics]] working group on the topic of the foundations of quantum theory. In 1980 Kraus spent a sabbatical year at [[University of Texas at Austin|UT Austin]] with [[John Archibald Wheeler]], Arno Böhm, [[George Sudarshan]], [[William Wootters]], and [[Wojciech Zurek]].

Karl Kraus died in 1988 at age 50 from the effects of cancer.<ref>Georg Reents: ''Nachruf auf Karl Kraus'', Foundations of Physics Letters, Vol. 2, S. 7, 1989.</ref>

== Work ==
Kraus work focused on the connection between the [[quantum nonlocality|quantum non-locality]] and the [[Principle of locality|locality]] of the classical world. He did work on this topic covering the [[Einstein–Podolsky–Rosen effect]]<ref>Karl Kraus: ''Quantum Theory, Causality and EPR Experiments'', in Proceedings of the Joensuu Symposium on the Foundations of Modern Physics: 50 Years of the EPR Gedankenexperiment, p. 138, World Scientific, Singapore, 1986.</ref> and issues regarding the [[measurement problem]] in quantum theory, a problem which, in his opinion, was largely ignored in the [[Copenhagen interpretation]] by the founders of quantum theory.

Some of Kraus' important publications on the measurement problem in quantum theory were:

*Measuring processes in quantum mechanics I: Continuous observation and the [[quantum Zeno effect|watchdog effect]].<ref>{{Cite journal

| journal = Foundations of Physics

|bibcode = 1981FoPh...11..547K }}</ref>
*Measuring processes in quantum mechanics II: The classical behavior of measuring instruments.<ref>{{Cite journal
| doi = 10.1007/BF00738299
| issn = 1572-9516
| volume = 15
| issue = 6
| pages = 717–730
| last = Kraus
| first = Karl
| title = Measuring processes in quantum mechanics. II. The classical behavior of measuring instruments
| journal = Foundations of Physics
| date = 1985-06-01
|bibcode = 1985FoPh...15..717K }}</ref>
*States, Effects, and Operations.<ref>{{Cite book

=== Kraus representation and Kraus operators ===
In his 1983 book ''States, Effects, and Operations'', Kraus described the measurement process in quantum mechanics for the first time using the concept and mathematical formalism of a [[quantum operation]], a special class of [[Map (mathematics)|maps]] of [[density operator]]s. The representation he used for these maps is now known as the Kraus representation, [[Kraus operator|Kraus operator]] formalism or operator-sum formalism, and is now frequently used in the field of [[quantum information]]. The Kraus representation is based on [[Stinespring dilation theorem]] about [[completely positive]] images of finite-dimensional [[C*-algebra]]s.<ref>W. F. Stinespring, "Positive Functions on C*-algebras", ''Proceedings of the American Mathematical Society'', 211–216, 1955.</ref> For a modern proof of the Kraus representation, which is based on [[Choi's theorem on completely positive maps]]<ref>{{Cite journal
| doi = 10.1016/0024-3795(75)90075-0
| issn = 0024-3795
| volume = 10
| issue = 3
| pages = 285–290
| last = Choi
| first = Man-Duen
| title = Completely positive linear maps on complex matrices
| journal = Linear Algebra and Its Applications
| date = June 1975
| doi-access = free
}}</ref> instead of Stinespring's set, see ''[[Quantum Computation and Quantum Information]]''.<ref>{{Cite book
| publisher = Cambridge University Press
| isbn = 978-0-5216-3503-5
| last = Nielsen
| first = Michael A.
| first2 = Isaac L.
| last2 = Chuang
| title = Quantum Computation and Quantum Information
| date = 2000-10-23
| url = https://books.google.com/books?id=65FqEKQOfP8C
}}</ref>

The issues discussed by Kraus regarding the foundations of quantum theory are still a current area of research. New theoretical advances are discussed in Erich Joos, [[H. Dieter Zeh]], Claus Kiefer, Domenico Giulini, J. Kupsch, I.-O. Stamatescu.<ref>{{Cite book
| publisher = Springer
| location = Berlin
| isbn = 978-3-5400-0390-8
| last = Joos
| first = Erich
| first2 = H. D.
| last2 = Zeh
| first3 = C.
| last3 = Kiefer
| first4 = D.
| last4 = Giulini
| first5 = J.
| last5 = Kupsch
| first6 = I.-O.
| last6 = Stamatescu
| title = Decoherence and the Appearance of a Classical World in Quantum Theory
| date = 2003-05-13
| edition = 2nd
| url-access = registration
| url = https://archive.org/details/decoherenceappea0000unse
}}</ref> These decoherence theories have been combined with modern experiments, particularly those done by the groups of [[Serge Haroche]] at Paris and [[Anton Zeilinger]] at Innsbruck, Vienna), in an attempt to use the measurement process in quantum theory to better understand relationship between quantum and classical world.<ref>{{Cite book
| publisher = Springer
| isbn = 978-3-540-35775-9
| last = Schlosshauer
| first = Maximilian A.
| title = Decoherence - and the Quantum-To-Classical Transition
| location = Berlin
| series = The Frontiers Collection
| accessdate = 2014-01-18
| date = 2007
| url = https://www.springer.com/physics/quantum+physics/book/978-3-540-35773-5
}}</ref>

In addition to mathematics and physics, Kraus had a special interest in biology, acquiring an extensive knowledge on the subject and even publishing some biological work.<ref>G. Reents, B. Schiekel: ''In memoriam Karl Kraus''.</ref>
